Voronoi Kolam

Kolam
Sona
Networks
Nodes and Edges
Eulerian path
Hamiltonian Path
Published

November 23, 2026

Modified

November 23, 2026

Introduction

A good way to view Kolam construction is to take a parent-child sort of operation: we plot the Voronoi diagram of the grid of points, and then following Gopalan[], we selectively remove some of the boundaries of the Voronoi. We can also add an artistic dimension, but “curving out” the trajectories so that they encircle the pulli-s rather than dart past them.

Step 1: Voronoi of a general grid

If we plot a grid of points on a square grid, then it should be clear that the Voronoi boundaries of the assemblage of points is simply the perpendicular-bisectors of the segments joining adjacent points. See Figure 1 below:

  • With R
  • With p5.js
Show the Code
pts <- expand.grid(x = 1:5, y = 1:3)

ggplot(pts, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_voronoi_tile(aes(fill = interaction(x, y)),
    bound = c(0.5, 5.5, 0.5, 3.5),
    colour = "white", show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_voronoi_segment(bound = c(0.5, 5.5, 0.5, 3.5), colour = "black") +
  geom_point(colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(title = "Rectangular Grid with Voronoi Boundaries") +
  theme_minimal()

Step 2: Random Modification to Voronoi

If we were to randomly drop Voronoi boundary edges between some pairs of adjacent points, we would get something like this:

  • With R
  • With p5.js
Show the Code
set.seed(42)

pts <- expand.grid(x = 1:5, y = 1:3)

# Vertical edges: separate horizontally adjacent points (4 x 3 = 12 edges)
v_edges <- with(
  expand.grid(x = 1:4, y = 1:3),
  data.frame(
    x = x + 0.5, xend = x + 0.5,
    y = y - 0.5, yend = y + 0.5
  )
)

# Horizontal edges: separate vertically adjacent points (5 x 2 = 10 edges)
h_edges <- with(
  expand.grid(x = 1:5, y = 1:2),
  data.frame(
    x = x - 0.5, xend = x + 0.5,
    y = y + 0.5, yend = y + 0.5
  )
)

edges <- rbind(v_edges, h_edges)

# Randomly keep ~60% of the interior edges
drop_prob <- 0.4
edges <- edges[runif(nrow(edges)) > drop_prob, ]

# Outer bounding rectangle (always kept)
rect <- data.frame(xmin = 0.5, xmax = 5.5, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 3.5)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = rect,
    aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
    fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges,
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Grid Voronoi with random boundaries removed",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  )

Step 3: Let there be light and mirrors

Now let us pretend that these boundaries are double-sided mirrors. And further that as mathemagicians, we can we insert a ray of light diagonally into any cell and watch it bounce around.

The resultant light paths could look like Figure 3:

  • With R
  • With p5.js
Show the Code
# ---- 1. Mirror layout (same construction as the previous chunk) ----------
make_edges <- function(seed = 42, drop_prob = 0.4) {
  set.seed(seed)
  v <- with(
    expand.grid(x = 1:4, y = 1:3),
    data.frame(x = x + 0.5, xend = x + 0.5, y = y - 0.5, yend = y + 0.5)
  )
  h <- with(
    expand.grid(x = 1:5, y = 1:2),
    data.frame(x = x - 0.5, xend = x + 0.5, y = y + 0.5, yend = y + 0.5)
  )
  e <- rbind(v, h)
  e[runif(nrow(e)) > drop_prob, ]
}

# ---- 2. Ray tracing ------------------------------------------------------
trace_loops <- function(edges, nx = 5, ny = 3) {
  # Keys for the surviving interior mirrors
  vert <- edges$x == edges$xend
  keep <- c(
    sprintf("V%.2f,%.2f", edges$x[vert], (edges$y[vert] + edges$yend[vert]) / 2),
    sprintf("H%.2f,%.2f", (edges$x[!vert] + edges$xend[!vert]) / 2, edges$y[!vert])
  )

  is_half <- function(a) abs(a - round(a)) > 0.25

  # Apply the wall at point p to direction d (reflect if mirror, else pass)
  interact <- function(p, d) {
    if (is_half(p[1])) { # vertical wall at x = p[1]
      m <- p[1] %in% c(0.5, nx + 0.5) ||
        sprintf("V%.2f,%.2f", p[1], p[2]) %in% keep
      if (m) d[1] <- -d[1]
    } else { # horizontal wall at y = p[2]
      m <- p[2] %in% c(0.5, ny + 0.5) ||
        sprintf("H%.2f,%.2f", p[1], p[2]) %in% keep
      if (m) d[2] <- -d[2]
    }
    d
  }

  chord_id <- function(p, d) sprintf("%.2f,%.2f", p[1] + 0.25 * d[1], p[2] + 0.25 * d[2])

  # Every cell has 4 chords (a diamond); each is a possible starting segment
  starts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nx * ny), function(k) {
    i <- (k - 1) %% nx + 1
    j <- (k - 1) %/% nx + 1
    data.frame(
      px = c(i - .5, i, i + .5, i), py = c(j, j + .5, j, j - .5),
      dx = c(1, 1, -1, -1), dy = c(1, -1, -1, 1)
    )
  }))

  used <- character(0)
  loops <- list()

  for (s in seq_len(nrow(starts))) {
    p0 <- c(starts$px[s], starts$py[s])
    d0 <- c(starts$dx[s], starts$dy[s])
    if (chord_id(p0, d0) %in% used) next

    p <- p0
    d <- d0
    path <- list(p)
    repeat {
      used <- c(used, chord_id(p, d))
      p <- p + 0.5 * d
      d <- interact(p, d)
      path[[length(path) + 1]] <- p
      if (all(p == p0) && all(d == d0)) break
    }
    loops[[length(loops) + 1]] <- data.frame(do.call(rbind, path)) |>
      setNames(c("x", "y")) |>
      transform(loop = length(loops) + 1)
  }
  do.call(rbind, loops)
}

# ---- 3. Run and plot -----------------------------------------------------
edges <- make_edges(seed = 42, drop_prob = 0.4)
paths <- trace_loops(edges)
paths$loop <- factor(paths$loop)

cat("Number of closed light loops:", nlevels(paths$loop), "\n")
Number of closed light loops: 10
Show the Code
pts <- expand.grid(x = 1:5, y = 1:3)
rect <- data.frame(xmin = 0.5, xmax = 5.5, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 3.5)

ggplot() +
  geom_path(data = paths, aes(x, y, colour = loop, group = loop), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_rect(
    data = rect, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
    fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour = "black", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), colour = "grey40", size = 1.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Closed light paths bouncing between two-sided mirrors",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  )

This is almost a kolam! But not monolinear! How can we make it more like a kolam?

Step 4: Bend the Light

Let’s bend the laws of physics and bend the light to reflect off the mirrors using bezier curves, rather than straight lines! Here is what we might get Figure 4:

  • With R
  • With p5.js
Show the Code
# ---- Curved reflections: reuses `paths`, `edges`, `pts`, `rect` ----------
stopifnot(exists("paths"), exists("edges"), exists("pts"), exists("rect"))

# Largest achievable gap for a given curvature (see notes)
max_gap <- function(curvature) 0.25 - 0.1875 * curvature

# Round off one closed loop. v: data frame x, y (last row repeats the first)
curve_loop <- function(v, s, w, n) {
  v <- as.matrix(v[, c("x", "y")])
  v <- v[-nrow(v), , drop = FALSE] # drop duplicated closing point
  N <- nrow(v)
  prv <- c(N, seq_len(N - 1))
  nxt <- c(2:N, 1)
  d_in <- (v - v[prv, ]) / 0.5 # direction of arriving chord
  d_out <- (v[nxt, ] - v) / 0.5 # direction of leaving chord
  t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = n)

  out <- vector("list", N)
  for (k in seq_len(N)) {
    m <- v[k, ]
    if (all(d_in[k, ] == d_out[k, ])) { # ray passes through: no bounce
      out[[k]] <- matrix(m, nrow = 1)
      next
    }
    P0 <- m - s * d_in[k, ] # curve leaves the incoming ray
    P3 <- m + s * d_out[k, ] # curve rejoins the outgoing ray
    P1 <- P0 + w * (m - P0) # control points pulled toward
    P2 <- P3 + w * (m - P3) # the mirror point by w
    out[[k]] <- outer((1 - t)^3, P0) + outer(3 * (1 - t)^2 * t, P1) +
      outer(3 * (1 - t) * t^2, P2) + outer(t^3, P3)
  }
  res <- do.call(rbind, out)
  res <- rbind(res, res[1, ]) # close the loop
  setNames(as.data.frame(res), c("x", "y"))
}

# gap       : distance from the mirror to the apex of each curve (grid units)
# curvature : 0 = straight chamfer across the corner, 1 = fully rounded bend
curve_paths <- function(paths, gap = 0.05, curvature = 0.7, n = 25) {
  stopifnot(gap >= 0, curvature >= 0, curvature <= 1)

  s <- 4 * gap / (4 - 3 * curvature) # setback along the rays
  if (s > 0.25) { # neighbouring bounces would collide
    warning(sprintf(
      "gap %.3f too large for curvature %.2f; using max gap %.3f",
      gap, curvature, max_gap(curvature)
    ))
    s <- 0.25
  }

  pieces <- lapply(split(paths, paths$loop), curve_loop, s = s, w = curvature, n = n)
  out <- do.call(rbind, Map(
    function(d, id) {
      d$loop <- id
      d
    },
    pieces, names(pieces)
  ))
  out$loop <- factor(out$loop, levels = levels(paths$loop))
  out
}

# ---- Run and plot --------------------------------------------------------
curved <- curve_paths(paths, gap = 0.1, curvature = 0.75)

ggplot() +
  geom_path(data = curved, aes(x, y, colour = loop, group = loop), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_rect(
    data = rect, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
    fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour = "black", linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(data = pts, aes(x, y), colour = "grey40", size = 1.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Curved reflections off two-sided mirrors", x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Notes:
# Gap: this is the perpendicular distance from the mirror to the apex of the curve, in grid units where neighbouring points are 1 apart. gap = 0 reproduces the sharp geometric bounce.
# Curvature: at 0, the corner is cut by a straight chord with two abrupt kinks. At 1, the bend is spread out into a smooth arc. The curve is tangent to the incoming and outgoing rays for any curvature above 0.
# Limit on the gap: each chord has a bounce at both ends and is 0.5 long, so each curve can start at most 0.25 from its mirror point. That makes the maximum gap 0.25 - 0.1875 * curvature, which is 0.25 at curvature 0 but only about 0.06 at curvature 1. Larger requests are clamped with a warning. If you need bigger gaps with round bends, the bounces would have to be spaced further apart, for example by using a coarser mirror grid.
# Topology: the loops and the cells they fill are unchanged, because the curves replace only the vertex geometry, not the tracing. So all 15 cells are still covered, and the loop count printed earlier still applies.

Discussion

  • A kolam is a curved rendering of a Voronoi Diagram of a set of points
  • By modelling the Voronoi itself as a set of doubles-sided mirrors, we get the starting point to generate a kolam for a set of points
  • We can then insert light into the grid, and watch it reflect off the mirror-walls of the Voronoi.
  • If we retain the full Voronoi, we will get diamonds of light around each point
  • If we *remove parts of the Voronoi , then the light rays can travel over longer paths, before returning to form some sort of closed path
  • And if we make the reflections curvy using bezier curves, that is the kolam, albeit not necessarily monolinear

Design Process

  • Generate a set of points on a square grid;
  • Enclose these in a logical boundary shape ( rectangle in the above diagrams );
  • Generate the Voronoi diagram for the points, and bound the Voronoi with the enclosing shape;
  • Remove parts of the Voronoi, where you want the kolam-light-path to continue. Here lies the artistry! Try to remove these in a symmetric fashion
  • Re-run your code to let the light travel over the new set of paths
  • There!!

Wait, But Why?

  • There are many ways to creating symmetry and shapes
  • For Kolam and Lusona, we have seen matrices, mirrors, knots, and voronoi diagrams as vehicles to visualize and create them
  • Which method do you like the most?
  • What is unique about each method?
  • How are they related? ( of course!!)
